analysis.one_liner: Combines mortgage-relief insurance, housing counseling, and fraud funding with legal shields for mortgage servicers and banks.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the troubled HOPE for Homeowners program with a new FHA insurance program to refinance mortgages of homeowners in default or underwater, created a permanent HUD Office of Housing Counseling with $45 million a year in grants, made the $250,000 bank deposit insurance limit permanent, and funded 30 new FBI agents to fight mortgage fraud. It also gave mortgage servicers a legal safe harbor to modify loans without being sued by investors, barred the Treasury from taking voting common stock when buying assets under the TARP bailout, doubled the tax rate on gains from selling a home that received federal relief, and imposed citizenship and income-accuracy conditions on receiving any relief.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in default or owing more than their homes are worth would get government-insured fixed-rate refinancing with prepayment penalties waived; 2009-2010 homebuyers would get a refundable credit of up to $10,000; bank depositors would get permanent $250,000 insurance; counseling nonprofits and fraud enforcement would be funded. Mortgage servicers gain a lawsuit shield, and banks gain expanded FDIC and NCUA borrowing authority.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces HOPE for Homeowners with a program insuring refinanced mortgages for owners in default or underwater, with fixed rates, terms up to 40 years, and waiver of prepayment penalties and default fees [S3].
Creates a HUD Office of Housing Counseling and authorizes $45 million a year for fiscal 2009-2012 for counseling grants to states, local governments, and nonprofits [S3].
Authorizes $31.25 million for 30 additional FBI agents and 2 dedicated Justice Department prosecutors to combat mortgage fraud, plus task forces in the 15 highest-fraud areas [S3].
Makes the $250,000 deposit insurance limit permanent and raises FDIC borrowing authority from $30 billion to $100 billion and NCUA authority from $100 million to $6 billion [S3].
Allows a refundable general homebuyer credit of up to $10,000 for residences purchased in 2009 or 2010, scaled to down payment size [S3].
Gives servicers a safe harbor from investor lawsuits and repurchase obligations for loan modifications that meet default-foreseeability and net-present-value tests through 2011 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the refinancing insurance program and the refundable homebuyer credit, and the bill cuts $1 billion from TARP funds to offset program costs. Homeowners who accept assistance must share a percentage of their home's future appreciation with the government and pay a doubled tax rate on gains from selling the subsidized residence.

drawbacks.text: Section 10 removes the exclusion of gain on sale of a principal residence for anyone whose home received relief under the bill and taxes such gain at twice the normal rate, a penalty that would discourage participation [S3].

Section 12 conditions any relief on verifying that the borrower's income was accurately stated on the original mortgage, that the home is a principal residence, that the borrower was never convicted of financial fraud, and that the borrower is a citizen or legal permanent resident [S3].

The servicer safe harbor overrides investment contracts, blocks investors from forcing repurchase of modified loans, and requires losing litigants to pay the servicer's attorney fees, reducing accountability to mortgage-backed securities investors [S3].
Section 9 bars Treasury from receiving common stock or exercising stock voting power in TARP purchases, giving up taxpayer upside and government influence over bailed-out firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The foreclosure-relief, counseling, and fraud-enforcement provisions would have helped ordinary homeowners in the middle of the housing collapse, and the deposit-insurance and servicer safe harbor provisions had plausible public benefits of their own. But the bill's design pulls against itself: the doubled capital-gains tax on assisted homes and the strict eligibility conditions would narrow who actually gets relief, while the servicer liability shield and the ban on Treasury taking common stock tilt accountability away from the financial firms whose lending caused the crisis. It is a mixed package, and its parts would have worked at cross-purposes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to three House committees the day it was introduced, a piece of it was sent to a Judiciary subcommittee in August 2009, and no committee ever reported it or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Judy Biggert introduced the bill on March 4, 2009, with 31 Republican cosponsors including the top Republican on the Financial Services Committee [S5, S4].
It was referred the same day to the Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees [S5].
On August 19, 2009, the criminal-law portion was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security; that was the last recorded action [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and financial institutions faced no new modification mandates, no TARP common-stock or dilution requirement, and no tax changes, because the bill never advanced. Homeowners in foreclosure got no new help from this bill, though other federal programs operated that year.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Republicans in a House where Democrats held 253 of 431 seats; the bill died in committee without any roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill shields servicers from investor lawsuits and repurchase claims when they modify loans, which clears legal obstacles to helping distressed borrowers but also removes a check on servicer conduct and shifts litigation costs to investors. Sources: [S3]

Permanent $250,000 deposit insurance and expanded FDIC/NCUA borrowing authority backstop the deposit funds; this protects banks from runs and protects ordinary depositors at the same time. Sources: [S3]

industries.industry: Financial firms receiving TARP bailout funds
industries.note: Barring Treasury from taking common stock or warrants that dilute control means bailed-out firms keep full private ownership and taxpayers forgo the upside and oversight that equity stakes provide. Sources: [S3]

Servicers could modify loans regardless of investment contracts, could not be forced to repurchase modified loans, and winning lawsuits against servicers would trigger fee-shifting, so investors bear the cost of modification decisions. Sources: [S3]
A new HUD Office of Housing Counseling and $45 million a year in grants would fund counseling organizations serving homebuyers and renters. Sources: [S3]
A refundable credit of up to $10,000 for homes purchased in 2009-2010 would stimulate home sales. Sources: [S3]
